It could have been a policeman, because we tried to locate you because we had the feeling that you had vanished. So it may have been a policeman who turned up at your door to check where you were. Why are you telling that somebody tried to kidnap you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This young woman who came to my door, she was a female, and she's here. She's not a member of the Serbian police. (redacted) (redacted). But why did she come to my home? Why was the Trial Chamber mistrustful when I always responded to telephone calls? Mr. President, there were at least 300 telephone calls over the past two or three years from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Why would that name be redacted from the transcript? (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (redacted) They have now been arrested in Pristina. Now, why should this be a secret, why the conspiracy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, you're on your feet. What do you have to say, because apparently Mr. Seselj anticipated what you were going to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... witness unit made arrangements to provide transportation for Mr. Stefanovic for his appearance today. I am, I'd say minimally, a little bewildered by the conspiracy theory being created or that the Victim and Witness Unit, the officer who provided transportation would create an assassination attempt or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What sort of transportation?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the person who came to see you, and we'll have to redact her name, is a staff member of the Registry. She came to see you to make arrangements about your transportation. We are not talking about an agent of the German intelligence services. It was simply someone who was doing her job. Please do not develop any kind of conspiracy theory about all this. It was just an employee of the Registry who was there to help you, as part of your testimony. We're going to redact her name, because she's entitled to protection from the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... just pass over this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Seselj repeated --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't allow you to declare me paranoid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you told us that someone came to your door. I immediately wondered who could have come to get you, especially since earlier on you told us that somebody had tried to kidnap you. But apparently the person who came to see you is a staff member of the Registry. She didn't come to see you to kill you. She just wanted to ask you to go to the office, and this was following a request made by the Judges or the Trial Chambers. They wanted to see you -- we wanted to see you. We have nothing against you. So if you believe immediately that someone who is doing her job, who comes to see you to tell you that you are going to testify, if you immediately jump to the conclusion that someone is trying to murder you, then we're indeed faced with a slight problem. Okay, we've clarified this point. There's no danger you're under. Ms. Dahl, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two more words. We can't just pass over this just like that. What sort of transportation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you want to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said I'm paranoid. I'm not paranoid. I left my home to go in the direction of the Tribunal. I've been living in Belgrade for 35 years, so why would someone need to transport me from here to there, across the River Sava? It's less than two kilometres away. Who is going to believe that an employee should come over from Sarajevo to transport me? Maybe I'm crazy, all right, but don't ask me to be clever.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You are not being candid with the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For half an hour -- to be sane for half an hour and then crazy for another half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, you are not being candid with the Court, are you? You and I and my investigator had a telephone conversation last Tuesday, where you told me and my investigator that you had made arrangements with the Victim and Witness Unit to be picked up in time for your testimony today. You were not surprised, were you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have that recording? I wasn't surprised, but my family was. They alarmed my friends. I hadn't taken a mobile phone with me. You are trying to portray certain things here in a negative light, as far as I'm concerned, and you're not allowing me to explain. It's nothing terrible. Let me explain how it happened. And you say, "Keep quiet, don't talk, calm down, you'll die here," I don't know what. I left my home. I went out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stefanovic, let's put that aside for the time being. Ms. Dahl reminded you that she called you on Tuesday and she told you that a car would come and fetch you to take you to the office for the videolink testimony, and because of that, somebody came to see you. There's nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That wasn't how it was. Excuse me, that's now how it was, Your Honour. Madam Dahl has her conversation with me recorded. I received a subpoena on Friday from the Serbian police. It was my mother's Patron Saints Day, it was the feast day, the Holy Arcangel. And I was summoned to report to the Tribunal at 1.00. And the lady who telephoned me -- every keeps telephoning. Nobody wants to send a fax or an e-mail or communicate in a civilised way. They always call from a no-number telephone, and then they ask whether I'm there, and then it's whether I said something or not. Madam Dahl has that conversation on tape. Last Tuesday, I was in the office of my lawyer, Zoran Stojkovic, and we overlooked the fact that Friday was the Holy Arcangels' Day. That's a family feast day which -- St. Michael, and that's the day when the whole family gathers together and nobody leaves home. I was supposed to be at home. But I apologised to Madam Dahl for that reason, and I said that the OTP had no need to contact me because I had sent written information to Judge Dilparic about my status and to the Tribunal in The Hague so there was no misunderstanding. And you have the conversation on tape. I did not agree to have it taped, but if you do have it, play it now. I agree to have it played, the conversation on Tuesday between myself and the Prosecutor, Madam Dahl.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stefanovic, we have no recording, and it's not a common practice to record all telephone conversations. I, for one, do not have any recording at my disposal. So you are asking for this recording. We don't have a recording.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... conversation and I said don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm interested in, and it's also in the interests of Mr. Seselj, what I'm interested in is for us to go back to the topic of the Serbian Radical Party. That's the purpose of your testimony. Ms. Dahl, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have a comment to make. I'm not interested in Seselj -- in the interests of Seselj, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, please put your questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I got an answer to the question about whether Mr. Stefanovic had been threatened with death in or before 1994 which caused him to remain in his position as secretary-general longer than he wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, did you or did you not receive a death threat from Mr. Seselj at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I can explain, but you're not allowing me to explain what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Chamber's permission, I'd like to move on to the activities during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You mentioned before the break that the Radical Party was interested in securing publicity and popularity for itself. Did you have the occasion to accompany Mr. Seselj when he gave speeches in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, and it's quite normal that the party wanted as much publicity as possible in order to attract the largest possible number of voters. Every party does the same, both the Democratic and Republican Parties in America and the National Front in France, and any European party, they all want to attract as many voters as possible in order to get the biggest piece of pie they can in the elections. That's the reason why parties exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, when you went with Mr. Seselj in 1991, when he gave different speeches, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Wherever they invited us or where it was in our interests to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you travel in a place --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: To --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- that Mr. Seselj referred to as Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade, the term "Eastern Slavonia" is something everybody uses, not just Seselj. You are probably referring to the villages around Vukovar, Vinkovci and so on. That's probably what you're referring to. The answer is, yes, there were occasions when I went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That region refers to areas that are presently in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're trying to say by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm trying to get the geography.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: They're part if Europe, if Croatia enters.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you give the Trial Chamber the gist of Mr. Seselj's speeches --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: "Eastern Slavonia," in Belgrade, is a term that's commonly used.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Chamber's permission, may I put some leading questions to the witness to see if we can get through this bit about geography?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please proceed. We'll try to save time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Is the area referred to as Eastern Slavonia located within present-day borders of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When Mr. Seselj made speeches in 1991 within the area called Eastern Slavonia, was he -- how did he describe the land vis a vis Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just add to clarify some things to you. Seselj and I promoted the party in Vienna also, and we said the same things in Vienna that we said in Eastern Slavonia. It was a very similar speech, presenting the party platform. Seselj drew the attention of the local population to the fact that they should not allow the genocide from 1941 to 1945 against the Serbs to be repeated, and he pointed out that this genocide could happen again. Quite simply, he said they should not allow the Ustasha to take them to the killing fields and to camps once again. Maybe that's what made this speech different from other speeches, but I felt that this was quite natural, quite normal. I supported that policy. Privately, personally, I'm on bad terms with Seselj, but I cannot deny his policy. I cannot challenge his policy. I still support it. It would have been wonderful if Croatia had not committed genocide either in World War II or now, if they had not expelled the Serbs from their age-long halves and expelled them from the territory. What would happen now if the French were to get up and expel the Germans from Alsace or some other region? I can give you 150 examples. The Southern Tirol, for example, Italy is paying the Germans for remaining to live in Italy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, let's stay with the history and the time period we're discussing, please. Did Mr. Seselj, in giving those speeches, say that the area called Slavonia was Serbian land?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I seem to have got caught up in these wires here. Let me just take a moment to disengage myself. Well, what do you mean by your question? That's the fact today. It's Serbian land. The Croats expelled the Serbs. My country is -- I apologise. What belongs to me is Aleksandar Stefanovic's land. That's my property, and I have land in the village of Zabari, near Valjevo, and that's my land, it's called my land. Now, if there was some land belonging to some man Pantovic, and if there's a whole village of Serbs, then it will be Serb land by the same token.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, do you need to take a break? I notice that you are coughing.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was there a War Staff within the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Sir, before we move on to the War Staff, which is a very relevant issue, one question. You said that you went along with Mr. Seselj when he gave speeches. Do you remember when Mr. Seselj went to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So you can't tell us anything about that. It's just a matter I wanted to clarify. Ms. Dahl, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was there a War Staff within the SRS?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you recall when it was created?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was created when the need arose for a number -- with a number of people who were from Serbia wanted to go -- well, through their own personal motives, their ethnic affiliation, to go and try and help those Serbs over there who were under threat by the Croats, so that this War Staff was the result of the need to transfer people who wanted to go, well, if I can say, the battle front and who did not have the means to do so, nor could they be transported or transferred to those war areas without somebody's help, so that that War Staff was a transmission -- well, it wasn't a nice name, "War Staff," but actually it was just a branch or section for where people would report to -- from Nis. [Indiscernible] 17 people would then be transported to Belgrade. They would be accommodated there and be given food, and then they were sent -- well, not in the sense of being sent, but -- I'm not quite familiar with the work of the War Staff. But, anyway, they were sort of sent to the Army of Yugoslavia or told to contact the barracks of the Army of Yugoslavia, and then the army organised this later on. I don't know what it did. But it was this transmission, like a transmission between the people who wanted to help the Serbs in jeopardy in those war-engulfed areas and the Army of Yugoslavia -- yes, let me say that, or Army of Yugoslavia barracks and so on. But, anyway --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: To your recollection, was a War Staff --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Special attention to that was paid by --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stefanovic, let me ask the next question. Was the War Staff created after the incident at Borovo Selo in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I don't know why that should be important. The War Staff was led by Ljubisa Petkovic. He was in charge at first for conducting a humanitarian mission, which was, in fact, assistance and help that these people required. So he was in -- or all people who were in exile.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Petkovic's deputy?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic's deputy was Drazilovic, Zoran Drazilovic, I think. Drazilovic, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In Mr. Petkovic's capacity as head of the War Staff, to whom did he report within the SRS?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: It's like this: You're now trying to lead me to say that it was Seselj and then that Seselj wielded influence and was the number-one man. What I'm trying to tell you is how things actually stood, and this is how they were. A really humanitarian organisation -- I can call it that, yes, I can, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I am answering your question, that's precisely what I'm doing. So this section or branch called the War Staff started off as a humanitarian organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, I had a specific question. In his capacity as head of the War Staff, to whom did Mr. Petkovic report within the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: Petkovic was the vice-president of the Serbian Radical Party, so he could not have reported to me. He had to report to the president. There was only the president that was superior to him, so that's logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who was the president?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: But I think -- Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You mentioned that the War Staff was recruiting people who wanted to assist the Yugoslav Army. Can you tell me how they did that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I explained that three or four minutes ago. These 20 young men and girls or whatever, a group of people, Serbs, whatever you like to call them, from the interior of the country, come to Belgrade, and then they knock at the door of the Serbian Radical Party and ask for assistance so that they could reach Slavonia or wherever, some area that was engulfed by the war. And at that point, Ljubisa Petkovic, I suppose, probably took us to Bubanj Potok and handed them over to the Army of Yugoslavia. So that is that, in simple terms. What I want to do is to explain to you how the War Staff came into being. It was envisaged first as a really humanitarian organisation which would assist, first of all, refugees from those areas, and I remember that full well. I remember a priest from Pakrac, a Serbian Orthodox priest. His name was Dragan. And with a young, petit wife, he came --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... because we do not have unlimited time, and I want to focus on the recruitment of volunteers and the transferring of individuals to the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: It's like this: There was no recruiting by the Serbian Radical Party, no recruitment, and I say that with all responsibility. Nor did any of these, well, conditionally speaking, volunteers go through having been influenced by the Serbian Radical Party at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I want you to take a look at paragraph 16 of your statement, the first sentence that reads: "The SRS War Staff started recruiting volunteers after the Borovo Selo incident in May 1991." Can you find that sentence in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me just read through that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you find the sentence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I analyse this paragraph 16? This is the first time that I -- can I just take a moment to analyse it?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, tell me if what I read appears there at paragraph 16, first sentence.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: What it says here, well, I have a slight correction to make in the first sentence, those first two lines, and then after that everything is correct as it states here.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Which correction --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a bit distorted, but for the most part correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What correction do you want to interject to the first line or first two lines?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to explain this to you, but you don't want to listen, you don't want to hear me, to help you to understand what the function of the War Staff was. It is true that when I go there in the morning, I would find people there from various parts of the country, and then they would be taken to the park over there where Seselj made his speeches. Now, whether he was careful in what he said or not, well, I never heard Seselj incite people to go, let alone do anything else, so that's -- or kill people, but -- so that can remain, that other part, but these first two lines are the ones that need correcting.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... correction, so what is it, because I need to bring your attention to another sentence and I want to move on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's rather an unwieldy interpretation in those first two lines, unfortunate interpretation, but you don't want to hear me. The War Staff was not an SS division, it was a humanitarian organisation which really did rally -- well, not go around collecting, in that sense, just as in our poem about the little girl picking strawberries, but, anyway, the volunteers came there and -- well, not volunteers, actually. They were just people -- well, we refer to them as volunteers, but they were just people who wanted to go and assist those Serbs under jeopardy in the war-engulfed areas. Otherwise, everything else is correct. And Seselj -- well, not only Seselj, but they would gather together in the park, and then he would say --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can I ask you to stop, please. I want to turn your attention to the paragraph immediately above that, in the middle, paragraph 15 in the middle. It says: "The role of the War Staff was to recruit volunteers and send them to the front-line on behalf of the JNA, although I am not aware of any official agreement between the JNA and SRS." Does your statement say that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, here --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, I want a "yes" or "no," not a, "Well, look." Either the statement says that or it doesn't. Please answer the question that's presented to you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: For me to answer -- well, I can't give you a yes-or-no answer. I can explain it to you, explain everything it says here and what the truth of it was, but I can't just give a yes-or-no answer, because it's both "yes" and "no," the answer is both "yes" and "no," and I'll tell you what the "yes" is and what the "no" is in just a moment, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, the statement says --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: If you're interested, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In paragraph 15, the statement says: The role of the War Staff was to recruit volunteers and send them to the front-line on behalf of the JNA, "although I am not aware of any official agreement between the JNA and the SRS." That's what the statement says; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says here, that's how it's written, but I can't say that that's how it was. The fact of the matter is that this act of people arriving to the premises of the Serbian Radical Party you refer to as recruitment, whereas it's quite a different action altogether, and I would describe it in different terms. The people that come to the premises of the Serbian Radical Party were, yes, that's true, sent on to the JNA or the Army of Yugoslavia, whatever it was called, and I have no idea whatsoever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Witness, we're losing time here. I'll go to the point. This War Staff, in your view, did it have an operational function? In other words, was it controlling the volunteers on the battlefields or was the role of the War Staff only to send volunteers who would come to the premises? In other words, does that mean that the War Staff had nothing to do with the combat operations? Please, please, give an answer to that question, and I think that would help everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The latter is correct, the latter part of your question. Let me repeat and clarify. What is correct is this: That the people came there, well, whether they were volunteers or whatever, people who wanted to help those Serbs over there, and it is also correct that the party would transfer those people to the JNA barracks and that every further supervision over those people ceased at that point. Now, what the army did, the army probably armed them, gave them uniforms, was in command of them on the battle front. If somebody was killed, they would send them back, and so on. Is my answer clear?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to make, Mr. President. If the Trial Chamber recalls, these questions were explained in detail during Expert Theunens' testimony and some other witnesses. This is -- well, now we're having the witness go through these things again, which he wasn't aware of at the time, that wasn't his competence, so let's not trouble him with that. And we know that the party sent volunteers to Serb villages in Slavonia up until September 1991. From September 1991, everything was under the JNA afterwards, and we've clarified that here a number of times, whereas we're giving the witness a hard time here with leading questions on the basis of a statement compiled by the OTP, and who knows under what conditions he put his initials to that, and that is what I mean when I say "giving the witness a hard time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, nobody's giving the witness a hard time, nobody's torturing the witness. If he was under torture, I'm sure he would be able to ask us to stop. I think he's provided an answer. What you've said was already said many, many times before. So please, Ms. Dahl, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: From your knowledge, working at the headquarters of the SRS, can you compare the volunteer units recruited by the SRS to the combat units of, for instance, the JNA, or the Red Berets, or Arkan's?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. What kind of question is that? The Red Berets or Arkan's men? That is impermissible. The Red Berets were never Arkan's groups, and when the Red Berets were established sometime in 1996, a number of former Arkan's men joined up, but the Prosecutor is making his own conclusion, that the Red Berets were Arkan's groups or troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I have the right to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... your question in such a way that the witness can provide an answer. Maybe you can ask him whether he knew that Arkan existed, whether he knew that there were particular units, and if he says "yes," then you may proceed on that basis. Witness, wait until Ms. Dahl rephrases her question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Based on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. May I be allowed to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you wish to say, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me, the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. You said, "May I be allowed to say something," so I'm asking you, what do you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Prosecutor came -- what was the person before Ms. Dahl? He was an American from Boston. What was his name? Anyway, he came, and he discussed this with me in detail, he talked to me in detail, and I explained that I was in charge of politics in the party, not the war or whatever else. So I can improvise, of course. It seems a bit -- it would be ludicrous for me to take Seselj's side and say, yes, that's how it was in September or whatever, because please believe me, I don't know about that. I don't know that any volunteers were sent up until September. If you want to believe me, then do. But what I heard from him, I don't think it goes to his advantage. Well, it does or it doesn't. I haven't followed this trial, so I don't know what is in his interests or not. But the fact that he just put forward, I say with full certainty that it is correct, but I couldn't remember it because at that time the Radical Party was engaged intensely on setting up boards in various parts of Serbia, and outside Serbia, too, in Europe, England, Germany, so that my involvement was towards setting up these various boards rather than sending these -- well, there's been a lot of speculation about what the War Staff is, and volunteers, and who is Ljubisa Petkovic going to beat. It was a humanitarian organisation. We took Ljubisa Petkovic, who was a man who was incapable of doing any army service. All he could do was to take them beans or potatoes or put up some -- accommodate someone from the war-infested area. Yes, it was called "the War Staff," but its function was not that. It was to feed people, to lodge people.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, did the JNA have the most disciplined combat units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? I was never up at the front. How should I know? You want me now to analyse this. I don't think it had the most disciplined units, or maybe it did. Maybe Arkan had better men, or whoever did. I don't really know. I didn't deal with war matters or an analysis of the war, an analysis of the JNA. Had I been a JNA commander, I would have taken Zagreb and Ljubljana in three days' time and solved the whole problem in Yugoslavia. The United States supported various proposals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please focus on the questions, because you say, "Had I been a JNA commander, I would have taken Zagreb in three days." Maybe, but that's not really the question. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You were interviewed in 2006 by members of the Office of the Prosecutor; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And you told them during that interview that the JNA had the most disciplined combat units; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what I said. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And in --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you expect me to remember what I told the investigators about the JNA after all this time?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Paragraph 15 of your statement says that: "The JNA had the most disciplined combat units." Doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what it says there, it says. As far as the most disciplined combat units were concerned, well, I suppose that's all right. What can I do? So my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And the SRS volunteers --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: And I think they ought to be the most disciplined.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And the SRS volunteer units were men of poor quality; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I meant is that they weren't officers, professional soldiers; they were ordinary citizens who had to go. If they went to war, they had to have some training. That's what I meant. I didn't mean to say that they were not brave soldiers. I think they were brave, but -- men, but they weren't trained properly. I didn't mean to say that they were weaklings.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What is a Chetnik vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a man who deserves to be a Chetnik vojvoda. It's a title, "Chetnik vojvoda," and that title is something that emerges from the traditions of the Serbian army, like a Superman, Tarzan.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Does Seselj appoint persons within the SRS to be Chetnik vojvodas?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. He didn't appoint me, and I'm sorry for that, and I'm angry at him because of that and all the rest of it, but I don't know much about that. They went to some village over there on Mount Romanija, a number of people went there. Perhaps they didn't deserve to be given these attractive titles, but they became Chetnik vojvodas over there. He had the right to promote people to vojvodas, since Momcilo Djuric promoted him to a Chetnik vojvoda. So all this was done with certain norms, customs, whatever you like to call them, that were in force among us Serbs and in the Serb army. So I don't see why I wasn't awarded that title.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Seselj appoint Ljubisa Petkovic to be a Chetnik vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I think he did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How about Zoran Drazilovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I repeat part of my answer? I didn't take part in that. I don't know what year that was. Anyway, they went to Bosnia and I stayed on in Belgrade. A group of men went there. I think you have a list of the names and surnames and middle names of the people who were given the title. I see that it says "19, Ljubisa Petkovic," and Zdravko Abramovic, Jovo Stojic, Tomislav Nikolic, Slavko Aleksic, Srecko Radovanovic, nicknamed Debeli, Tode Lazic, Branislav Vakic, Mirko Blagojevic, a whole list there, Branislav Gavrilovic, Manda. That's what it says in paragraph 19, so let me just read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Based on your interactions with Mr. Seselj while you were working at the party headquarters, did you have an opportunity to observe whether Mr. Seselj kept himself informed of activities of the party?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I informed him on a daily basis. He was very well informed about party activities, so of course he'll follow the activities and inform himself of the activities of the party. So my answer is, yes, he did follow the activities of the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you observe whether or not Seselj informed himself of the activities of the volunteers at the front-line?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, everyone in Serbia, especially people involved in politics, were very interested in what was happening at the war theatre, so Mr. Seselj was also interested, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to observe that Seselj was worried or concerned about the activities of the volunteers at the front-line?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: You know what? What do you mean "be concerned"? I don't understand your question, I don't understand your question. Excuse me, but I don't understand your question. Could you clarify what you want me to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In paragraph 19, your statement says: "I observed that Seselj was worried about the activities of the volunteers at the front-line." Perhaps, Mr. Stefanovic, you can clarify by what you meant in that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The Prosecutor is suggesting to the witness that the witness actually stated this. What he meant when he wrote this or, rather, what did the investigator mean who wrote this down? The investigator should be brought here to answer the question about what he thought when he was -- what he meant when he was writing this down. But now the Prosecutor is asking the witness what he meant when he stated that, instead of asking him, "Did you really say this?" This was all written down by the investigator. Every statement is written down by investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber observes that the witness makes statements. He explained that he was not in full agreement with what he originally stated. Now Ms. Dahl is putting questions to the witness in order to obtain some clarification. Ms. Dahl, you may proceed. I don't think you have much time left. I'll turn to Madam Registrar so that she tells us how much time you've got left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. Your Honour, you've just said something disastrous about me, or you may have the completely wrong impression. It's true, I couldn't say to you -- Your Honour, when The Hague Tribunal asked me to contact the Serb Radical Party and ask Seselj whether he wanted to come to Belgrade to be tried in Belgrade, and they said that he would not get more than ten years in jail and that he would be released provisionally as soon as the trial was over, I contacted Dragan Todorovic. I spoke to him in a cafe, a pizzeria cafe in New Belgrade, and I told him what the Tribunal wanted from Seselj. I told him to ask Seselj. A few days later, Dragan Todorovic came to see me, and he said, "Seselj rejected this in disgust. He doesn't want to be tried in Belgrade." And I told this to the representatives of the Tribunal, and they were surprised. They said, "What a fool he is. Why doesn't he want to do this?" I thought, and I still think, that all this is a farce, whether there was an indictment against Seselj when he left. Now they're asking was there a staff, was there not a staff. You say I made a statement and I don't agree with this statement. I did give a statement, and I agree with it, but there are some things in there that have nothing to do with what I said, especially these ridiculous paragraph numbers here, which are ridiculous. Whatever I say as a witness is being doubted.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me try to save some time, Your Honour. The witness stated dated 16 June 2006 includes a document table that records Mr. Stefanovic's comments and observations about the documents. I'd like to tender the 2006 statement with the document table and the associated documents. Several of them are already in evidence. I can conclude my examination, and Mr. Seselj can examine based on the statement, but I think that the witness has demonstrated that he does not adopt this statement. And we can lay the additional foundation of reliability that the Chamber might want through another witness, but the statement is what he told the representatives of the OTP that recorded the statement, and he's signed it and his signature is on every page in his own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, there are two statements, the 2003 and 2006 statements. Do you tender both?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: We tender the 2003, but it's subsumed completely within the 2006. I think it has the same indicia of reliability in the fact that the similarities corroborate each other, but the 2006 stands alone in its completeness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will give you the floor, Mr. Seselj, but first of all I would like to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, what would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's absolutely impermissible to admit the statement into evidence, because the statement was not written by the witness. The statement was written by The Hague investigators. If the statement could be admitted into evidence, there would be no point in bringing any witnesses here or examining any witnesses. Then all the 103 or 4 witnesses could be dealt with in the same way. Their statements could be admitted into evidence, and we would get it all over with. This is all very cheeky. This is very impertinent. You're putting in statements under 92 ter, 98 bis, 92 quater, and so on and so forth, and this whole trial looks like a distance learning course. And these statements were signed by witnesses under God knows what circumstances, and this witness is demonstrating here under what sort of pressure he signed those statements, whether he wants to admit it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber, at the request of the Prosecution, decides to give two MFI numbers, one MFI number to the 2003 statement and another one to the 2006 statement. The Chamber considers that it is in the interests of justice, even if the witness challenges the very content of the statements. There was one in 2003 and one in 2006. The probative value of such statements will be assessed by the Trial Chamber at the end of the proceedings, in the light of other evidence, but of course you will have to ask for the document to be added to the 64 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order to upload the statements and make them available, they have 65 ter numbers 7416, which corresponds to the 2003 statement, and 7417, which corresponds to the 2006 statement, and we would ask the Court to add that to our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can we have two MFI numbers for both statements, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 7416 will become Exhibit P633 marked for identification, and 65 ter number 7417 will become Exhibit P634 MFI as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you asked for marked for identification numbers, whereas the Registrar has given you permanent numbers, as far as I was able to observe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. No, because on line 2, page 74, there's a reference to an MFI number. But please, Madam Registrar, could you please reconfirm that these are MFI numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Both exhibits are marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'd like to put into the record the 65 ter numbers that correspond with the document table so that the Chamber can consider whether to admit those documents, because they've been commented upon by the witness. 65 ter 239, 65 ter 369, 65 ter 404, 65 ter 416, 65 ter 431, 65 ter 433, 65 ter 436, 65 ter 473, 65 ter 990. The video material in the document chart relates entirely to 65 ter 6066, which is a transcript of Mr. Seselj's interview given to the filmmakers of "Death of Yugoslavia." 65 ter 1836, 65 ter 778, 65 ter 192, 65 ter 1816, 65 ter 1636, 65 ter 1800, 65 ter 1802, 65 ter 1108, 65 ter 1039, 65 ter 1829, and, finally, 65 ter 1018. I have skipped over the documents that Mr. Stefanovic commented on that have already been admitted into evidence. The document index at the front of our binders indicates which ones I've skipped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have MFI numbers for all these documents, Madam Registrar. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, where did the witness comment on these documents? Where did he state his position on them? You never accepted anything like this previously. This is the first time you've done something like this. And, secondly, by admitting these witness statements into the file, this is something that no Trial Chamber has ever done in the history of this Tribunal, which I think is the worst tribunal that has ever existed anywhere in the world. It only happened in the case of Slobodan Milosevic because there was no one there to protect his procedural rights, because Mr. Milosevic dealt only with the merits of the case and there was no one to be concerned about his procedural rights. The Prosecutor even made up Rule 29 bis and a half because the Rules 92 ter and 92 quater did not exist at the time. You can look at the transcript of that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Could I respectfully request the Chamber to ask Mr. Seselj to lower his voice, because I cannot hear the translation because of the volume of his speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we've taken note of your observations. This is the reason why we're asking for an MFI number to be given to those documents. It doesn't prejudge in any way our final decision. Madam Registrar, please, can we have MFI numbers for all these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 239 is now Exhibit P635. 369 is Exhibit P636. 404 is Exhibit P637. 416 is Exhibit P638. 431 is Exhibit P639. 433 is Exhibit P640. 436 is Exhibit P641. 473 is Exhibit P642. 990, Exhibit P643. 6066 is Exhibit P644. 1836 is Exhibit P645. 778 is Exhibit P646. 192 is Exhibit P647. 1816 is Exhibit P648. 1636 is Exhibit P649. 1800 is Exhibit P650. 1802 is Exhibit P651. 1108 is Exhibit P652. 1039 is Exhibit P653. 1829 is Exhibit P654. And 1018 is Exhibit P655. All of them marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, you've completed your examination-in-chief, then. Witness, before the break, I have a number of quick questions to put to you in order to supplement some of your answers. As of today, I understand that you are running a company, but are you still in politics or have you stopped altogether?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm still involved in politics, and you're right, I'm at the head of a company. But let me say one thing. I see that there's a lot of fuss about something, and I can clarify some points for you, something that would make it much clearer about these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me stop you here. What I'm interested in is your involvement in politics. You've just told us that you are still involved in politics. In what party, in what political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently, I'm not involved in a political party, but two or three years ago, with a friend of mine, I established a party called Hrast, meaning "oak." It's not established in the electorate. But I'm involved in politics at a lower level, at the level of municipal committees and so on and so forth, but that's something that one cannot bypass in these times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In your view, when did you leave the Serbian Radical Party, when did you distance yourself from Mr. Seselj in 1996? Why, for what reason? For political reasons, for personal reasons, because you didn't get along with him anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was -- well, how can I classify it. It was neither personal, nor did it have to do with the party platform. It had to do something with staffing issues, where I was bypassed and overlooked, and I think that was the reason for our disagreements, which led me to leave the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I listened to your explanations about your function as a secretary-general, I had the feeling that you did not have any actual political role, you were dealing with purely administrative matters. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a large influence on the organisation of the party on press conferences, which were very important. It's very important in the party to get as much media support as possible, to hold as many rallies as possible, to have as many appearances on television and radio broadcasts and in the media as possible, so that my role was by no means small. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You remained in your -- in that position of secretary-general until 1995. During that period from 1991 to 1995, you know better than anyone else that a number of events took place. Did you receive any information according to which volunteers of the SRS committed crimes? And if that is the case, what measures did you take at the highest levels of the party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still think that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party did not commit any crimes. They knew nothing about crimes, nor were they able to commit crimes. They were mostly under the command of the army and the local people there, the Territorial Defence or whatever it was called, and I don't know that a single member of the Radical Party committed a crime. Had we known about this, I would have been the first to react and to report that person, but I have no knowledge of that. In my statement, which I have never seen before, I am sure I said at least ten times to the investigators that I did not know of a single crime committed by Vojislav Seselj. Why doesn't Madam Dahl want to talk about her meeting last year? Does it say that in the statement or not, because I didn't read that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't have this document, and that's to do with your relations between yourself and the Prosecutor and it's not relevant. I read your statement with great interest, however. You're challenging the veracity of your statement, but nonetheless I had the feeling that at the beginning of the Serbian Radical Party, you had an important role to play within that organisation. I read, for example, that you organised a symbolic trial of Tito, and you stated that Mr. Seselj drafted the indictment against Tito. You explained that this was done to do away with the cult of personality around Tito. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did that take place? Did that take place after Tito or while he was still alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was ten years after Tito's death, but the personality cult of Tito still existed in Yugoslavia. There was a law on the protection of the name and work of Tito. You couldn't say that the existing regime was no good, because they would immediately take out these paragraphs, put them on the table, and say, "You spoke against Tito, and that's a crime under paragraph this and that." You had to remove the cult. Mao Tse-tung had a cult, Tito had a cult. Even if they die, the cult persists. After the death of Mao Tse-tung, China did not change course politically or in any other way. The existing regime could not be removed until Tito's cult was removed, because there was a law under which you could not criticise the existing system. Do you understand me? There was a law on the protection of the name and work --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. There's maybe one topic where you could be very helpful to us. I'm talking about the relationship between Milosevic and Mr. Seselj. If you were asked to define this relationship, were they good relations or rather difficult, politically speaking? What is your feeling about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look here. If you want me to be quite honest and open, we have to go back to the beginning of my testimony, when they tried to persuade me, when I said, "Hello, Prime Minister, I don't know that Seselj committed a single crime." He said to me, "You don't have to talk about crimes. Go and discredit him politically. Go and discredit him politically." And that was a task assigned to me, that I should say something bad about him. And now, Judge, I'm looking at these points this lady gave me. I'm looking at points 21 and 26. Only a madman could say things like that. In paragraph 26, it's all invented, from "A" to "Z". This is the first time I've read my statement, so I cannot state my position on it in the way that you and Madam Dahl are doing. I just read points 21 and 26, I scanned them, and what it says here in 26 I could have only said if I had gone completely mad, because as for Jovan Marijanovic, I never saw him, and Bozidar -- General Bozidar Stefanovic is a man I've never seen in my whole life. And now it says here that they were political allies, and this tells me everything I need to know, Judge. I've only read this paragraph now. General Domazetovic, I don't know if Seselj knows him at all. Frenki Simatovic, of all people, I only met him a few years ago. I did sign and I'm telling you, if they had told me then, "Go and discredit him," what could I do? Seselj is a very decent man. Had I said that, they would have said, "You've gone crazy." They said, "Go and discredit him," I don't know of any crimes that he committed. I'm asserting here that he did not commit any crimes. I'll probably never speak to Seselj again in my life, but I'm telling you he's not a criminal when he was telling people off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please explain something, something in relation to what you stated in 2005 about assassination projects instigated by Mr. Seselj. You, yourself, supposedly stated that you had been threatened. Why did you make such a statement in 2005, on the 4th of August, 2005?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll explain that in detail to you. It was like this, here's why I said that: When I saw what the Tribunal wanted and my role in discrediting Seselj, then an idea came to me, and that is that some generally-known facts which the papers wrote about, which were on television and so on, I -- that I was asked to say, yes, that's what Seselj did, or I would say that, but those were individual things. The killing of Pasko, Slobodan [as interpreted]. After that incident, I became interested about that killing and came by a file which the Belgrade -- dossier which the Belgrade police compiled about the killing of Pasko Jovic, and it still exists here in Belgrade at the police station, and it said that a maniac, a sexual maniac, perpetrated that killing and then had intimate relations with this dead woman. I don't want to talk about that here, but Jovic had at least 15 interviews saying that Seselj had killed his wife, and then he involved me and engaged some policemen, heaven knows what. And then I skillfully went and said that -- well, I said that the grounds for that story were erroneous and that Jovic made false accusations against Seselj with respect to Pasko, and I said, "Well, there's this other man who is accusing Seselj of killings." Now, as far as his threats to me, they were uttered by someone else. I don't have direct knowledge of this. Somebody who was angry and arguing with Seselj wanted to influence me and persuade me to say things against Seselj and undertake certain acts and so on. So this is secondhand information. It's not my direct knowledge. I conducted an investigation, large-scale investigation, about the killing of Pasko, and I came to these conclusions, so I'm not denying what it says here. I did say all that, but with a certain intention in mind and not these silly things that it says in paragraph 21. I don't know what it says otherwise. If I were to take over all these documents, I would have to look at them and then say what I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You accused Mr. Seselj with respect to a number of murders or assassinations, and because of that you were granted protective measures. But when you did all this, what was your purpose? Who were you trying to help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A service -- well, not a service, it was a type of conditioned order by the president of the government of Serbia, the prime minister of Serbia, and the then Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal, Carla Del Ponte, because I talked to Dr. Zoran Djindjic about this directly, and he said, "You'll never appear as a witness in The Hague, I guarantee that, but go and clear things up. These people have not understood anything. They started gritting their teeth and so on."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand properly, you're telling us that the former prime minister, who later was murdered, he's the one who asked you to make a number of statements to accuse Seselj; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Politically compromise Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to break for 20 minutes. We'll resume at 10 past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The court is back in session. My fellow Judges have a number of questions to put to the witness before we proceed to the cross-examination by Mr. Seselj. Witness, Mr. Seselj will not be in a position to complete his cross-examination today. You will have to come back tomorrow for the hearing at 2.15. You will have to go back to the location where you are currently, and obviously we'll make sure that your expenses are covered by the Tribunal. Before I give the floor to Mr. Seselj, I believe that my fellow Judges have questions to put to you. Judge Lattanzi first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, could you talk to us about your current relationships with the members of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this: I always -- I was always on good terms with some members of the Serbian Radical Party, and I still am today. With others, I'm not on good terms, so I didn't revive our relationship and didn't have -- have not have a good relationship. For example, Tomislav Nikolic, we had an argument and we're still estranged to the present day, although we are next-door neighbours, so to speak, in our residential building. I am "kum" to Dragan Todorovic, so I always maintained good, intimate "kum" relationships, regardless of what arguments we might have through the Assembly, or through the papers, or other -- in other media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you recently met with members of the Serbian Radical Party? Have you had private conversations with any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At least on two occasions, I was on some property owned by Dragan Todorovic. He has some very good wine, so I was on his estate and we drank wine once. And Jelica Radeta was with us on one occasion, and Dragan and I had a bottle of wine to drink. Well, we each had a bottle of very good white wine. Otherwise, I was invited to speak at a meeting organised by the Radicals, and then I met just in passing a large number of those Radicals. And this meeting took place in the Trade Union Hall a month ago. But that was a scientific meeting at which I presented -- it was nothing special. I presented my views on why the West had these sentiments of hatred towards the Serbs, and the main thesis was that without conciliation between the Western states and the Serbs, there would be no peace in the Balkans, after the terrible crimes committed by the Germans from 1939 to 1945, which history attests to. But Germany rose from the ashes, so to speak, so -- whereas us Serbs were betrayed 150 times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you. Sir, there's something I would like to know, something else, if it's possible. Have you met with some of the members of Mr. Seselj's Defence team? It would be rather natural if you had done so. Have you met any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I met a lawyer called Jerkovic, and I think he might be on the Defence team. But we did not discuss the Seselj trial at all, nor did we discuss anything -- any other things which were linked to this specific case, because, well, I don't know what he could tell me or what I could promise him. We discussed quite different matters. A friend of mine needed a service done on the territory of Zemun municipality, so that's what I wanted to ask him about. Now, as for these meetings, I don't know who's in the team. I know Maja Gojkovic; Vucic-Milkovic; Krasic, Zoran, used to be -- I think there's this man Jerkovic, too. I don't know who else is on his team. So there was no specific discussion between me and any of the Radicals in the sense of discussing the trial or anything. So when I saw that things had gone astray, that I might be thrown into prison like Ljubisa Petkovic, I engaged Zoran Stojkovic, a lawyer, because I saw that matters had come to a head, that Jerkovic was taken from the asylum and taken to prison, whereas Haradinaj was -- there was direct cooperation between Haradinaj and the OTP until he liquidated all the witnesses and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how I see things. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stefanovic, you told us during your testimony that in your view, the War Staff of the SRS was a humanitarian organisation. I think that's the expression you used. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At the beginning of its establishment, it was created to act in the way that would come under the heading of humanitarian organisation; that is to say, that's how I see it, humanitarian work, assistance, help in food, medicines, help to people in the war-engulfed area, and dealing with the repercussions of refugees and people coming in, women and children mostly, from the war-affected areas. And then later on it was as I described it, something that was -- well, assisted people to go there. And I was never a member of the War Staff, and I never meddled in affairs where my place was not. That was done by Ljubisa Petkovic. He was there. So you're extracting every last drop out of me, but I can only assume, if I see what the investigator wants, he says -- he says something to me, then I nod my head, so that -- and agree, so that I can be allowed to go home as soon as possible. But I'm under oath here now, so I say with full responsibility that it was established, and I know that at first all the assistants did go through this so-called War Staff. Now, it wasn't a humanitarian organisation, as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But as secretary-general of the SRS, I guess you would have been involved in assistance to the victims, the Serb victims, those members of the SRS who fell victims to the war at the front-line. That is to say, I suppose you would be involved in the provision of medicine to the wounded SRS members and volunteers at the front-line, as well as to assistance to the victims' families back in Serbia or Belgrade, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never. I never collected any humanitarian aid. All I dealt with was party business. It was Ljubisa Petkovic and the others around him, Zoran Drazilovic and another group of people, men and women around him, dealing with that kind of work exclusively. It would be silly for me to go around collecting medicines when I wasn't able to deal with the workload I have. And please believe me when I say I got up at 6.30 in the morning and went to bed after 11.00. I lived in the Excelsior Hotel and the Slavija Hotel, that's where I slept, and I knew the exact time I got up and went to bed. And I remember that in 1991, with my own car, it was a Ford Fiesta, I think, anyway, I drove 130.000, over 130.000 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, let's focus a bit on the assistance that the SRS, either through the War Staff or through some of its other channels, was able to provide to the SRS volunteers who fell victims or to those victims' families. I'm curious to know if you can tell us anything about if and to what extent the SRS was able to provide assistance in the form of medical care, hospitalisation, or other forms of assistance to the members -- to the volunteers who were wounded at the front-line or to these people's families. That's what I would like to know, because even though if you were not directly involved in that, I would assume that you at least knew about it, being the secretary-general of the party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Superficially, yes, so my -- that's a very good question. But you're forgetting one thing. All the Serbs -- you're characterizing all Serbs as members of the SRS. Mostly, those people -- well, none of them were members of the SRS. If women and children arrived, you don't ask them whether they're members of the Radical Party or whatever other party, and usually they weren't -- these women weren't members of any party, but they were provided assistance. Now, you shouldn't raise it to the level of hospitalisation and things like that, not at that level, to provide serious medical care, but, yes, they did get some sanitary material or things that were stored in warehouses, where the -- there was an expiry date that had -- a date that it had expired, so we provided them with some of those medicines. So I would otherwise be improvising if I told you more, because I wasn't really well-versed in this kind of humanitarian work, I wasn't involved in that side of things, but I knew that a group of women who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, I only want you to tell us what you know, and please do not speculate. So you're telling us that the SRS was somehow assisting by providing medicine and maybe other sorts of supplies to the volunteers that the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Food, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- that the SRS had facilitated to the front-line? Do you understand my question? Maybe I'm not putting it very clearly, so I'll try once again. I'm sorry. You told us earlier on that the SRS was facilitating and helping, assisting, people who came to the SRS headquarters and wanted, by their own will, to be sent to the front-line in order to help against the Serbs who were in trouble out there, and so I suppose that the SRS would then feel some sort of responsibility for the persons that they helped to get to the front-line, the volunteers who may or may not have been members of the SRS. But at least I suppose that there was some sort of registration. And then my assumption is, and I want you just to confirm or to deny, my assumption is that the SRS would feel some sort of responsibility for these people, so that if they were wounded at the front-line, then the SRS would, by virtue of its humanitarian assistance or otherwise, help them out; either to send them medicine, or if they needed to go to hospital, then see if they could facilitate that, or even if some of these persons were killed, then to help out with their families back home, and that's what I want you to explain a bit to us, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I fully understand your question. I think that you're idealising things. That organisation was not an ideal one. They weren't fronts like the Magino [phoen] line, 300 kilometres on the one side and the Medical Corps and so on and so forth. This was sporadical journeys of people, whether they were members of the party or not. Many of them no, but they were volunteers or, rather, people who wanted to protect the Serb nation. And all of them, including the Radicals and all the other parties, looked benevolently upon them, and that's what happens everywhere in the world when people go to war to help their fellow compatriots, to stay in their own homes, on their own threshold and so on, their own hearths and so on. Now, when I say "assistance," well, you asked the question, I remember a number of times that I bought sandwiches to feed the people who came to the Party premises and spent the night there and were hungry, so I went off -- I personally went off and, with my own money, bought them sandwiches. Now, do you consider that to be assistance to the War Staff of the Radical Party, or how you're going to assess this, I don't know. That's what I did. Anyway, with respect to people being killed, I can't tell you exactly who transported the dead. I think it was the army that was the main organisation, because we Radicals did not have the logistics at the front. You need radio stations, medical corps, vehicles, ambulances, or any kind of vehicles to transport men, especially if they're dead and you have to transport coffins across borders and so on and so forth. Anyway, that was the kind of support, and that's how I see it today. And I think it's quite normal. Now, whether there were any mistakes or not, I don't know, but I wouldn't have acted differently even today. If I went back to those years, I think that I did the right thing. And I say with full responsibility that Seselj didn't influence anybody and prevail upon them to go to the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, take it easy. Just listen carefully to the questions that I'm putting to you. You said that the SRS would provide coffins if some of them had been killed, and you also said that they would provide transport in order for the volunteers, I suppose, to go to the front-line, and if they were wounded, then to get back from the front-line. So my question is: Now, you have substantiated your answer a bit more. You said that they did provide medical assistance, they did sometimes provide coffins if somebody had been killed, they provide transportation to and back from the front-line. And before I move on, I just wanted to confirm, is this correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me check. You're talking about the volunteers who were killed at the front-line; is that right? Is that what you're referring to, just to see that I've got it right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. The SRS volunteers or at least the volunteers who came through the SRS headquarters and were sent to the war front with the assistance by the SRS, those people, if they were killed, did the SRS or could the SRS then provide some sort of assistance, for instance, by getting a coffin, or getting in touch with the family, or otherwise providing support and assistance to those who had been -- who had taken off to the front-line through the SRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand the question, and I'll be precise now in giving you an answer, very precisely and correctly. It's like this: All the people who were killed at the front, it was Zoran Drazilovic who was in charge of them. He represented the party. He would go to inform family members that their relative had died, had been killed. Now, if he had the resources, then the party did all this, it organised the coffin, the burial and everything else, the funeral. That comes under human solidarity, the heading of human solidarity. If not, then it would be the state or the army who would see to that. So that's as far as I know. I never attended any funerals, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And please just confine your answers to the questions that I'm putting to you, because we should not take up too much time. Mr. Seselj is waiting to get on with his cross-examination. Do you know if any of the volunteers were paid by the SRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't think the Radical Party financed the volunteers by giving them money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if they --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it did. I'm not quite sure, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's very fine. I'm satisfied with the answer. Do you know if the SRS was able to provide them with uniforms or weapons before they went to the front-line or as they were going to the battles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know, and I think that is -- was certainly the case, especially when it comes to weapons and uniforms, it was exclusively the JNA who would provide those. We didn't have any weapons or anything like that, so that's the assumption. We didn't have any uniforms or weapons, so we couldn't provide them with that, but the army did -- if they did, they would provide them with that. But, Your Honour, please believe me when I say that I never crossed the Sava or Drina Rivers from 1991 to 1995 more than twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm only interested in hearing what you knew or what you can tell us about what happened. I'm not implying that you traveled around and saw the battlefield. That is not my interest. The interest in my initial questions here have been to illuminate a bit the responsibility that the SRS felt for the people who went to the front-line, to the battles, through the SRS, and I think you have answered these questions as best -- as well as you could. Now, my next question would be: If the young volunteers who went to the front-lines were subjected to war crimes committed by, say, Croats or Muslims, or war crimes committed by the other side against the members of the SRS or against the volunteers who were at the battle and the front-line through the assistance of the SRS, would that be something that would be discussed or be addressed by the SRS? Do you know that? I'm speaking about war crimes committed against your people, against the volunteers, and my question is if any such crimes were reported to the headquarters of the SRS in order to be addressed at some other level, perhaps passed on to the military police of the JNA or passed on to somebody else, but was that something that was recorded or discussed in the SRS headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll be quite frank, Your Honour, to say that I never entered the War Staff, I never meddled in other people's affairs. However, what is the objective truth is that all those who were invalids, for instance, it was the state, well, as members of the military units of the official Army of Yugoslavia, most probably, I don't know for sure, but most probably they received some invalidity remuneration, some pensions or whatever. Now, as far as assistance to those people goes, I know that two of them were taken care of by the Radical Party, Dusica Nikolic and a man called Sima who fell casualty in some actions, but they were activists of the Radical Party before that, they were members beforehand and held important posts in the party, and when they returned to the party, too, as if nothing had happened. I don't know of other cases, but I came across many people later on who said that they had been volunteers, that they had been wounded, but it was mostly the state that took care of them, the army, I think. So I can't say anything other than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But my question was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there was no mention of that at any official meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, I understand. But at the meetings that you took part in in Belgrade, at the SRS headquarters, did the issue of war crimes committed against the volunteers ever come up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I don't think so. At least I don't know about them. That any item on the agenda was something like that, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
