utterances.text: So you never heard -- if I understand you correctly, you never heard that war crimes had been committed by the enemies to any of your volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I heard that many times, but it wasn't a discussion at any official meetings of the Serbian Radical Party. The Serbian Radical Party dealt with political issues, and it was those issues that were on the agenda of the Executive Board or the Central Homeland Administration or whatever. There was no discussion, as far as I remember, about, say, point 4 on the agenda would be war crimes against the Serbs, committed against the Serbs, as an item of the agenda. I don't think anything like that ever happened. Well, actually, I'm certain we didn't discuss it in that way. We dealt with political issues and matters at the official meetings. Otherwise, I had heard that terrible crimes -- terrible crimes had been committed in many instances, hundreds of them, both in Bosnia and Croatia. And a friend of mine, Dragan Jovanovic, was killed on the 19th of December, 1991, by the Ustashas, where they filmed it all on video, and then five or six years later I happened to see this, his killing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please understand me -- or, rather, I'm trying to understand you, because I don't see the coherence in this. If war crimes were committed on a large scale against Serbs, that would, I would imagine, be a very political issue in Serbia. I mean, you have spoken, yourself, during this testimony about the genocide that was committed against Serbs during the Second World War. So if anything of a similar kind would happen again against Serbs, that would be a political issue in any party in Serbia, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, that would be a national issue, par excellence, but political activity in Serbia was such that one could not prevent crimes by political action. One had to support the government that was promising to assist the Serbs in areas where they were under threat in order to help prevent crimes. That would have been the task of any serious political party. If Serbia was willing to help the Serbs escape crimes, then we would support the government that was promising that, and vice versa, but what you're asking is something new for me because I never attended a meeting where we discussed specific crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we understand each other perfectly well, and maybe I have not been clear enough. I'll try one more time, and then after that I only have two more questions for you and then I'm finished. My question to you, Mr. Stefanovic, was if -- the issue of the commission of war crimes, not any particular war crimes, but war crimes in general, committed by the enemy against volunteers, Serb volunteers at the front-line, was that not a political issue in the SRS, and how was it addressed if it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to reply to that, Your Honour. I think I've said everything. I've told you everything I know. If you think I'm concealing something, tell me what you're getting at. But to be quite honest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question was simple, and if you cannot answer, then you cannot answer and then we'll move on to something else. The next-to-last question I have is: Do you know if any of the volunteers who went to the front-line, if they signed up to become members of the SRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a difficult question again, because no official records were kept of this, but I think that when those people came to the party and stayed for an hour or two, it was not usual for them to sign up then and there and become members. They would become members or not in their local boards. We were a large party with a large number of members, and we did not insist that volunteers be members of the party. That's my answer. We did not insist that fighters be members, but some of the volunteers certainly were party members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last question I have to you relates to an issue that was brought up earlier by the Presiding Judge, and I caught sight of it because you have mentioned the same thing twice; that is to say, first in 2003, when you gave your statement to the investigator, and then again in 2006. So twice you have -- you raised the issue of the president of the SRS, Mr. Seselj, being worried somehow about the conduct of the volunteers at the front-line. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that, but if I did say that and if it's recorded, I don't know what the motive might be. Your Honour, I never saw this piece of paper before, the one on my left-hand side. I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Forget about what you think you saw and what you didn't see. If I can just, as an example, pop back to the statement you gave in 2003. In the English version, it's on page 14. It's towards the end of the statement, and it's under a heading that is called "Crimes Issues." And I read out from what was taken down in your statement. You were supposed to have said the following, and I quote: "I saw that Seselj was worried of the activities of the SRS volunteers, and he tended to prove that he was not responsible for the actions committed by the volunteers at the front-line." And that's all I would like you to expand a bit upon. What did you mean when you alleged or indicated or suggested that Seselj might have been worried about something that had happened at the front-line in which, apparently, SRS volunteers had been involved? What did you mean when you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When giving the statement, I've not been able to say this since the beginning of this hearing. I see you're all angry with me, the Judges, the Prosecutors and Seselj, all of you, you're all yelling at me. I'm not complaining, but forgive me for saying this. Believe me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, we are not angry at you and we are not yelling at you. I'm putting issues to you that you have raised yourself twice in 2003 and 2006, and there is no mystery about it. I just want you, because you're a witness and you're here to tell the truth and you're under oath, I just want you to tell us what you meant by saying what you said. That's all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that at all. Probably that is an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We've got ten minutes left. Mr. Seselj, maybe you could start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, in these 10 to 12 minutes, we might be able to clarify some minor status points. You said that the Serb Freedom Movement was established on the 23rd of January, 1990. Do you remember that the Serbian National Renewal of Mirko Jovic and Vuk Draskovic was established on the 6th of January, 1990?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Up to the point when Vuk Draskovic was expelled from the Serbian National Renewal, did this happen at the meeting of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down and not overlap. This is impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At the meeting of you, Dusan Boskovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're going too fast. The interpreters are asking you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You and Dusan Boskovic refused to join up with Vuk Draskovic, and Vuk Draskovic and I, on behalf of our parties, although he had been expelled and he was only pretending to be at the head of the Serbian National Renewal, signed an agreement on the establishment of the Serbian Renewal Movement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that in early June, Vuk Draskovic was replaced from the post of president of the Serbian Renewal Movement by a majority of votes after the scandal when the Saint Sava play was staged in the National Theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Kalinovica Piazza [phoen], is that the meeting you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 18 Nevesinjska Street?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are not yet a member of our party. Do you remember that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The witness is sitting in Belgrade, and unless you speak a lot louder, he won't be able to hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would be better if the witness was here, but what can I do about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that Vuk Draskovic, after he was replaced, established in the Rolex Restaurant a new party to which he gave the same name, the Serbian Renewal Movement, and then there were two parties having the same name?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then at the end of June, to avoid confusion among the public, we changed the name of the party from the Serbian Renewal Movement to Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that before the official registration of any political party?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was before the official registration of any party. There was not a single party that was registered at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Registration started in August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in August or September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your Liberal Party collectively joined the Serbian Chetnik Movement only then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you explained how the Serb Radical Party was established. You mixed up some functions, but that doesn't matter. Do you remember that as early as 1994, you put forward a proposal, at a meeting of the party leadership, that you be relieved of the duty of secretary-general and that we elect Aleksandar Vucic to that post because it transpired that he was talented for propaganda activities? Do you remember that meeting in my office?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what year it was, but superficially -- yes, I can't pinpoint the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. You were never dismissed from that post, but you yourself proposed that you be relieved of that duty, and I assert it was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I confirm that that's how it was, except that I'm not sure about the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we were wrong when we selected Aleksandar Vucic, but that's another issue. Do you remember that in 1997, in an informal conversation with a group of journalists in the Serbian Assembly, you said that you toppled the monument to Draza Mihajlovic, although that was not true? Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I do, but I think the year is not correct again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I remember it was in 1997, because I have a photographic memory. And then the journalists published this, and I summoned you and attacked you fiercely because you said this as a joke, but it was detrimental to the party; that's how it was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you quietly withdraw from the Serb Radical Party after that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were no conflicts; you simply disappeared. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify these few points if for no other reason than for this transcript, which will go down in history. Let me remind you of one more thing. Do you recall that this so-called War Staff was first called the Crisis Staff of the Serb Radical Party and it was headed by Ljubisa Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's silly to ask me about this War Staff. I don't know what the logic is and why you're all asking me about the War Staff. It's correct, I couldn't recall. I thought it was some sort of humanitarian work. I'm not sure. It was humanitarian work, or it can be described as activities which are usually referred to as humanitarian activities. And it's true that at the beginning, it was called the Crisis Staff, and I never poked my nose in there, and I don't know what they did or what they didn't do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic, there's no reason for you to become upset. The OTP has an abundance of documents showing that initially that Staff was engaged in providing humanitarian assistance, and then gradually it started sending volunteers. But do you remember that it was only in early October 1995 -- 1991 that the crisis --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: ... that the Crisis Staff was renamed into the War Staff of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely, the precise date, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you -- well, did I ever threaten your life? Did I ever threaten you with death?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did I ever threaten anyone's life?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I have to remind you now. I have to jog your memory, because the Prosecutor did the same. Do you remember that on one occasion, I threatened the Croatian Ustasha leader, Franjo Tudjman, and that for the Zagreb magazine 'Globus,' as a joke, I said that the Chetnik court had sat a court-martial and sentenced Tudjman to death and they published this as a serious piece of news?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that. It was the Chetnik corps, the collective body, not you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it was done for propaganda purposes and as a kind of joke?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember the statement that we -- that we Chetniks have river submarines and that we would take those submarines through the rivers to Zagreb and catch Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it was said that they would be sending them to Ljubljana also, and then they came to intervene and asked us not to send them to Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they made problems for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The priest Peran [phoen] in Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it was a joke?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR STEFANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm been given a single to slow down. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm really interested who else is with you in this room.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I'm demanding that the camera crew lift the camera and that he take a shot all around the room so that we can see who is in the room. Mr. Stefanovic, don't say anything. I want to see visually. I have the right to that, and nobody should get out of the room in the meantime. No one should leave the room in the meantime. Judges, is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you see me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I can see you and someone peeping behind you. Is that someone who's whispering what you should say? Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. What's your name?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to know the names of all those who are present in the Tribunal office in Belgrade in the course of this hearing. I have the right to that, and the public must know their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there is somebody with you. I guess he's the Registrar; right? Who is the person standing next to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you addressing me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could you tell us who's standing next to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a man sitting next to me. I don't know what his name is. You see now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This person is the Registrar. We know him very well. Are you reassured, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we going to find out the name of this person, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar. He's always here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you rejected my demand that the cameraman lift the camera and take a circular shot all round the room, span all round the room so we can see who is in the room?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, how many people are there in this room, because Mr. Seselj seems to be paranoid and thinks there's a conspiracy against him, so how many people are in that room where you are?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's me and another man. There are two of us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, paranoia is a dangerous mental illness. If I were suffering from paranoia, I would not be sitting here in the courtroom. So please refrain from such statements. I'm not paranoid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Stop this, Mr. Seselj. You are questioning the integrity of this Tribunal, suggesting that there were other people in the room than the witness. You were told there were two people. I asked the witness to confirm, and he did say that there were two people in that room. That's it. We will resume tomorrow, sir. We will resume this hearing tomorrow at 2.15. I will ask you to refrain from any contact with the media about these proceedings, and we will meet again tomorrow at 2.15. But be there at 1.00, because there are some technical checks to be done. I wish everybody a good evening, and we will meet again at 2.15.
